sources.title: Pearl
sources.accessNote: Read via the MediaWiki extracts API. Used for how natural pearls form (pearl sac, intruders, concentric layers) and which molluscs make them.

sources.title: Pearl of Lao Tzu
sources.accessNote: Used for the pearl's size, weight and origin.

sources.title: Evidence of Rotation in Flame-Structure Pearls from Bivalves of the Tridacnidae Family
sources.accessNote: Abstract and introduction read. Used for the non-nacreous structure of giant clam pearls, their flame structure, signs of rotation during growth, and their sizes.

claims.text: A natural pearl forms when a parasite, organic matter or an injury carries cells of the mantle's outer layer into the soft body. They form a pocket, the pearl sac, which coats the intruder with calcium carbonate and the protein conchiolin.
claims.evidenceNote: The encyclopedia describes the pearl sac and the usual triggers; it says the process is 'thought' to work this way.

claims.text: Despite the common belief, a grain of sand is rarely what starts a pearl.
claims.evidenceNote: Stated directly in the encyclopedia article.

claims.text: Like the shell, a pearl is calcium carbonate laid down in concentric layers, and the pearl sac grows by cell division as the pearl grows. An X-ray of a natural pearl shows a series of concentric growth rings.
claims.evidenceNote: The rings drawn in the cut pearl are far wider and fewer than the real layers, so they can be seen.

claims.text: All shelled molluscs can make some kind of pearl, but most are not gems. The lustrous nacreous pearls come mainly from pearl oysters and freshwater mussels.
Giant clam pearls are non-nacreous: porcelain-like, without nacre's rainbow sheen. They are built of crossed aragonite lamellae, which show a 'flame structure' and sometimes a silky shimmer.
claims.evidenceNote: GIA studied 37 pearls from the giant clam family (Tridacnidae), mainly Tridacna gigas, T. maxima and T. squamosa.

claims.text: Most giant clam pearls studied are symmetrical around one axis and show spiral patterns at their ends, which suggests they turn as they grow.
claims.evidenceNote: 35 of the 37 pearls had cylindrical symmetry; GIA reads this as suggesting rotation, not proving it.

claims.text: Tridacna gigas has yielded flame-structure pearls weighing several tens of carats, and very large concretions such as the Pearl of Allah, a blister pearl that grew against the shell and was cut from it.
claims.evidenceNote: One carat is 0.2 g, so several tens of carats is several grams. The drawn sizes of loose pearls are illustrative, not measurements.

claims.text: The Pearl of Lao Tzu (also called the Pearl of Allah), from a giant clam off Palawan in the Philippines, measures 24 cm across and weighs 6.4 kg.
claims.evidenceNote: Its early history rests on one owner's accounts, which the encyclopedia treats as embellished; the size and weight are not disputed. GIA gives about 6.37 kg.

claims.text: How long a giant clam pearl takes to grow was not found in the sources reviewed, so the slider shows sizes along the way, not ages.
claims.evidenceNote: A limit of this demo rather than a fact about the animal.
